source: Suri et al. (2023) Do LLMs show decision heuristics similar to humans? A case study using GPT-3.5 (anchoring, Study 1)
finding: ChatGPT shows an anchoring effect with a random-number anchor, close to humans.
numbers: Low anchor (10-20): ChatGPT mean 20.83 vs humans 22.50. High anchor (100-200): ChatGPT 105.97 vs humans 80.50. ChatGPT low vs high: t(58)=8.78, p<0.0001. GPT-4: 22.0 vs 94.33 (5 trials per cell).
limits: Small cells (30 per condition for ChatGPT); GPT-4 only 5 trials per cell; prompt began 'Pretend to be an agent that can do anything'.
agent_relevance: A number placed early in a prompt can pull the estimate. Keep unrelated numbers out of the working prompt; the program, not the model, should supply any reference figure.

source: Suri et al. (2023) Do LLMs show decision heuristics similar to humans? A case study using GPT-3.5 (framing, Study 3)
finding: Gain versus loss wording of a drug's efficacy changed ChatGPT's rating, with no variance across trials.
numbers: ChatGPT: all 11 trials gave 5 (gain frame) and all 11 gave 4 (loss frame), 1-7 scale. Humans: 5.2 vs 4.6, t(80)=3.86, p<0.001.
limits: Hypothetical doctor vignette; the model was near deterministic, so the effect looks cleaner than in humans. Authors suggest wording associations, not only loss aversion, drive part of framing.
agent_relevance: Framing works on the model through wording alone, so the same fact in gain or loss words may flip a verdict. Normalise task statements to neutral wording before the model sees them (S1 restatement).

source: Suri et al. (2023) Do LLMs show decision heuristics similar to humans? A case study using GPT-3.5 (representativeness, Study 2)
finding: ChatGPT fell for the conjunction fallacy in a Linda-like problem.
numbers: Conjunction option chosen 18 of 20 times by ChatGPT; humans in the classic Linda study: 85% chose the conjunction.
limits: The authors report the plain Linda prompt was evaded at first, so they rewrote it; results depend on prompt wording.
agent_relevance: The model follows vivid detail like people do. Probability estimates should come from code or counts, as G5 says.

source: Binz & Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3 (PNAS)
finding: GPT-3 on Kahneman and Tversky prospect-theory problem pairs showed 3 of 6 classic biases: framing, certainty effect and probability overweighting.
numbers: 3 of 6 biases found (framing, certainty, overweighting); 3 not found. Also a cab problem answer changed when only the option order changed.
quote: Simply changing the order of the options
limits: text-davinci-002 only; vignette tasks may appear in training data.
agent_relevance: Framing and ordering effects appear in the model's choices, so layout is a real lever and a real risk.

source: Jones & Steinhardt (2022) Capturing failures of LLMs via human cognitive biases (NeurIPS)
finding: Irrelevant preceding code plus a framing line makes Codex and CodeGen copy the framing line and lose accuracy.
numbers: HumanEval functional accuracy 32.9 (Codex) and 25.6 (CodeGen) originally; with irrelevant preceding functions plus a framing line it fell to 2.4-10.6 (Codex) and 1.5-11.0 (CodeGen). Framing line copied in 62.2-92.7% of Codex outputs and 58.2-79.3% of CodeGen outputs.
limits: Code models of 2021-22, not chat models; 'framing' here means irrelevant context, not gain/loss wording.
agent_relevance: Anything left in the context window is a possible anchor. Strip stale or unrelated text before each model call.

source: Jones & Steinhardt (2022) (anchoring, and use as a test method)
finding: Prepending a nearly-correct but wrong anchor function lowered accuracy and the output copied parts of the anchor.
numbers: Anchor functions lowered functional accuracy and raised the fraction of solutions containing the anchor's for-loop and print lines (Figure 4); exact values are only in the figure and were not read.
limits: Codex-era models.
agent_relevance: A cheap way to test a prompt layout: plant a wrong anchor and see whether it is copied. Usable as a layout test for our scaffold.

source: Zhao et al. (2021) Calibrate before use: improving few-shot performance of language models (ICML)
finding: Few-shot accuracy swings with the order of examples; GPT-3 has majority-label, recency and common-token biases. Contextual calibration with a content-free input ('N/A') fixes much of it.
numbers: Sentiment accuracy ranged from 54% to 93% across permutations of the same examples. Contextual calibration raised average accuracy by up to 30.0 points absolute.
quote: accuracy to vary from near chance to near state-of-the-art
limits: GPT-3 and GPT-2 era; classification; calibration needs token probabilities.
agent_relevance: Order and label balance in demonstrations are choice architecture for the model. Shuffle and balance examples in code; use a content-free probe to measure bias.

source: Zhao et al. (2021) (label balance and recency)
finding: An unbalanced prompt gives unbalanced predictions; ending the prompt with two Negative examples biases toward Negative.
numbers: Majority-label and recency bias shown on a balanced validation set; the variance stays with more shots and larger models (2.7B to 175B).
limits: Qualitative figure.
agent_relevance: The last item in the prompt carries weight. Put the real question last and keep examples label-balanced.

source: Lu et al. (2022) Fantastically ordered prompts and where to find them (ACL)
finding: The order of few-shot examples swings GPT-family accuracy from near random to near state of the art at every size tested; a good order for one model does not transfer to another.
numbers: Entropy-based order selection on a model-generated dev set gave 13% relative improvement across 11 text classification tasks. Sizes tested: 0.1B to 175B.
limits: Classification; older models.
agent_relevance: Do not hand-pick one fixed order. Randomise, or pick order by a label-free statistic computed in code.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Lost in the middle: how language models use long contexts (TACL)
finding: Accuracy forms a U shape by the position of the relevant document: best at start and end, worst in the middle.
numbers: GPT-3.5-Turbo, 20 documents: 75.8% when the answer document is first, 53.8% at index 9, 63.2% at last; closed-book (no documents) 56.1%, so a middle position is worse than no documents.
quote: performance is often highest when relevant information occurs at the beginning or end
limits: Early-2023 models; multi-document QA and key-value retrieval.
agent_relevance: Put the facts that matter at the start or end of the prompt, never in the middle. A direct prompt-layout rule.

source: Liu et al. (2024) (longer windows do not fix it)
finding: Extended-context versions of the same model show the same U shape.
numbers: Claude-1.3 (100K) vs Claude-1.3, 20 documents: 59.8% vs 59.9% at index 0, 57.0% vs 56.8% at index 9. GPT-3.5-Turbo (16K) 75.7% vs 75.8% at index 0.
limits: Early-2023 long-context models.
agent_relevance: More room in the window is not better recall of the middle; short curated prompts beat dumping everything in.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) Large language models are not robust multiple choice selectors (ICLR)
finding: LLMs prefer certain option letters (selection bias), mostly token bias on A/B/C/D. Moving the right answer to a given slot changes accuracy a lot.
numbers: 0-shot MMLU: moving the gold answer to D cut gpt-3.5-turbo from 67.2 to 60.9; moving it to A lifted llama-30B by 15.2 (53.1 to 68.2, passing gpt-3.5 at 65.3). With answers balanced at 250 each, llama-30B picked A/B/C/D 34.6/27.3/22.3/15.8% of the time. 20 LLMs, 3 benchmarks.
limits: MCQ with letter IDs.
agent_relevance: Never let slot position carry meaning. Permute option order in code and aggregate.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) (PriDe debiasing)
finding: Label-free debias: estimate the model's prior over option IDs by permuting options on a small test subset (for example 5%), then subtract it for the rest.
numbers: Evaluated on 20 LLMs; shown to transfer across settings. Exact gain figures are in tables not copied.
limits: Needs output probabilities.
agent_relevance: Code-side debiasing fits our rule that code, not the model, controls selection.

source: Pezeshkpour & Hruschka (2023) LLMs sensitivity to the order of options in multiple-choice questions
finding: Reordering options changes answers, even with few-shot demonstrations.
numbers: Performance gap of about 13% to 75% across benchmarks when options are reordered. GPT-4 example: prediction flipped from 'hen house' to 'outside bedroom window' on reorder (CSQA).
limits: Abstract and figure 1 read; mitigation numbers not recorded.
agent_relevance: Same lever as Zheng: option order is not neutral. Majority vote over shuffled orders is a cheap guard.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Large language models are not fair evaluators
finding: The order of two candidate answers changes the LLM judge's verdict; adding 'order must not affect your judgment' does not fix it.
numbers: Vicuna-13B beat ChatGPT in 66 of 80 queries with ChatGPT as judge when placed in the favoured slot. Conflict rate when order swapped: GPT-4 46.3% (Vicuna vs ChatGPT) and 5.0% (vs Alpaca); ChatGPT 82.5% and 52.5%. Calibration (evidence first plus swapped orders) lifted accuracy 9.8% (GPT-4) and 14.3% (ChatGPT); 20% human review cut annotation cost by 39%.
quote: Simply changing the order of candidate responses leads to overturned comparison results
limits: 80 Vicuna-benchmark queries; early-2023 GPT-4 and ChatGPT.
agent_relevance: A model judge must never see candidates in a fixed order. Score each in both orders and average in code. A written instruction to ignore order is not enough.

source: Sclar et al. (2024) Quantifying language models' sensitivity to spurious features in prompt design (ICLR)
finding: Meaning-preserving format changes (separators, casing, spacing) shift accuracy by large amounts; the effect persists with larger models, more shots and instruction tuning.
numbers: Up to 76 accuracy points spread for LLaMA-2-13B. GPT-3.5 across 320 formats: spread up to 56 points, median 6.4. Format ranking correlates only weakly between models.
limits: Few-shot, mostly open models, classification-style tasks.
agent_relevance: Report ranges across layouts, not one prompt. A hand-picked layout can move an arm by tens of points, a risk for our benchmark comparisons.

source: Allouah et al. (2025) What is your AI agent buying? (ACES): position and badges
finding: Shopping agents show large position effects in a mock store and the direction differs by model. Sponsored tags hurt; platform 'Overall Pick' badges help.
numbers: Conditional logit, Aug 2025 models; top row coefficient: Claude Sonnet 4 1.224, GPT-4.1 1.045, Gemini 2.5 Flash 0.344. Column 1: GPT-4.1 +1.122 vs Claude -0.297. Sponsored tag: -0.135, -0.248, -0.263. Overall Pick tag: +1.060, +0.802, +1.897. Scarcity tag: -0.076, -0.105, -0.342 (only Gemini significant). About 25,000 observations per model.
limits: Simulated store with eight products; six models; coefficients are a snapshot in time.
agent_relevance: Agents are nudgeable by layout and badges and a new model version can reverse the effect. Test layout on each model version, not once.

source: Allouah et al. (2025) (prompt fixes, headless, seller agent)
finding: Telling the agent to 'ignore position' attenuates but does not remove position effects; they persist in text-only JSON listings; model updates flip them; sellers can tune text to win.
numbers: GPT-4.1 and GPT-5.1 had almost opposite position biases. Gemini 2.5 Flash preview to release inverted bias from bottom row to top row. Seller GPT edits raised focal market share +3.66 pp (Sonnet 4), +8.37 (GPT-4.1), +14.79 (Gemini 2.5 Flash), +7.38 (Opus 4.5), +14.89 (GPT-5.1), +0.32 (Gemini 3 Pro, not significant).
quote: Explicitly prompting an agent to "ignore position" does not significantly mitigate position effects
limits: Mock environment; seller agent used competitor sales data.
agent_relevance: Instruction-only debiasing fails here, as in G1/G5. Randomise placement in code. Candidate text can be tuned to win selection, so treat it as adversarial.

source: Allouah et al. (2025) (rationality over model generations)
finding: Older agents missed simple dominating choices; newest models almost never do. Plain errors fell faster than layout bias.
numbers: Price test with a 1% discount: failures over 63% for Claude Sonnet 3.5 and 25% for GPT-4o; near zero for the latest. Rating +0.1 test: failure 28.7% Sonnet 4 and 15.1% GPT-4.1 (Aug 2025), below 1.7% for Dec 2025 models.
limits: Mock-store tasks with a clear best option.
agent_relevance: Capability gains remove plain errors but not layout bias, so a layout guard is still needed on strong models.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive bias in decision-making with LLMs (BiasBuster): bias findings
finding: Admissions decisions show framing and group-attribution bias in several LLMs; status quo and primacy effects were not human-like.
numbers: 13,465 prompts. GPT-4 admitted 40.5% more students under reject framing than admit framing. Llama-2 7B classified 32.1% fewer females as good at math. Status quo: all models except GPT-4 were inversely biased (the stated default option was chosen less).
limits: Admissions and math scenarios; one model and setup per figure.
agent_relevance: The default effect did not copy over from humans. Do not assume human nudge directions; test each.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) (mitigation methods)
finding: Zero-shot awareness prompts give small gains; few-shot debiasing can break instruction following; self-help (model rewrites the prompt to remove bias) works best.
numbers: Awareness mitigation made primacy distributions more uniform for Llama 2 and GPT-4, but self-help did better. Few-shot examples drove admit probability to 0 or 1 in some cases.
limits: Untested beyond admissions; exact table values not copied.
agent_relevance: Rewriting the prompt to neutral wording is safer than adding 'be unbiased'. Matches our restatement step.

source: Itzhak et al. (2024) Instructed to bias: instruction-tuned language models exhibit emergent cognitive bias (TACL)
finding: Decoy effect, certainty effect and belief bias are stronger in instruction-tuned and RLHF models than in their base models (Flan-T5, Mistral-Instruct, GPT-3.5, GPT-4).
numbers: Bias score = share choosing the target option in treatment minus control (example: 90% vs 70% gives 0.20). All option orders used. GPT-4 had lower certainty and belief bias, but its decoy effect rose.
limits: Scores averaged over products where some effects are not significant; decoy design copies US store prices.
agent_relevance: Alignment training may add nudge-style susceptibility. A stronger model is not automatically less nudgeable.

source: Macmillan-Scott & Musolesi (2024) (Ir)rationality and cognitive biases in large language models
finding: Seven LLMs are irrational on cognitive-psychology tasks, but mostly not in human-like ways, and answers are inconsistent across repeats.
numbers: Seven models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Bard, Claude 2, Llama 2 7b/13b/70b). Abstract: errors differ from human biases; large inconsistency in responses.
limits: Table 3 only partly read; per-model shares not recorded.
agent_relevance: Human bias lists are an imperfect guide to model errors. Test the model directly and repeat each item.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi & Kosinski (2023) Human-like intuitive behavior and reasoning biases emerged in LLMs but disappeared in ChatGPT
finding: Cognitive Reflection Test style tasks: earlier GPT models made human-like intuitive errors, ChatGPT and GPT-4 mostly did not.
numbers: Not recorded; not read for numbers.
limits: Unread; stated from title and memory. Do not cite numbers.
agent_relevance: Link to the dual-process subfield; check before use.

source: Horton (2023) Large language models as simulated economic agents: what can we learn from Homo Silicus?
finding: GPT-3 given social-preference and status-quo scenarios reproduced the direction of some classic behavioural-economics results.
numbers: Not recorded; not read for numbers.
limits: Unread; from title and memory.
agent_relevance: Compare with Echterhoff, who found status quo reversed for most models. Needs a check.

source: Synthesis: layout levers in the machine evidence (Zhao, Lu, Zheng, Pezeshkpour, Wang, Liu, Sclar, Allouah)
finding: Order, position, format and label levers move model choices by about 6 to 76 points, and an instruction to ignore them does not remove them.
numbers: Format spread up to 76 points (Sclar); option slot 6.3 down to 15.2 up (Zheng); judge conflict 46.3-82.5% (Wang); middle position 53.8% vs first 75.8% (Liu).
limits: Different models, tasks and years; Allouah shows the bias persists in 2025 agents.
agent_relevance: The prompt builder should fix a canonical layout, randomise orders in code, and keep key facts out of the middle.

source: Synthesis: which human nudges carry over to models
finding: Framing and anchoring carry over (Suri, Binz, Jones); the default effect did not in Echterhoff; badges nudge agents, scarcity tags mostly do not (Allouah).
numbers: Framing: ChatGPT 5 vs 4 on a 7-point scale. Status quo inverse in all models except GPT-4. Scarcity tag significant only for Gemini 2.5 Flash (-0.342).
limits: Setups differ; no study yet runs a matched default, ordering, framing and badge battery on one model.
agent_relevance: The human nudge list does not predict the model list. The SUBFIELDS item 3 pilot should include framing, order, default and badge arms.
